findings.description: The security group allows TCP/22 from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing SSH administrative access on a publicly addressable instance to the entire internet and enabling brute-force or exploitation attempts.
Port 80 is open to 0.0.0.0/0 and the instance serves plain HTTP (apache2 with no TLS configuration), so portal traffic crosses untrusted networks in cleartext.
The egress rule permits all protocols and ports to 0.0.0.0/0, providing no outbound segmentation and easing data exfiltration or command-and-control callbacks from a compromised host.

The user_data script exports a static AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in plaintext. User data is stored unencrypted, is visible in the Terraform state and console, and is retrievable by any process or SSRF vector on the host via the instance metadata service, leaking long-lived IAM credentials.

No metadata_options block sets http_tokens = "required", so IMDSv1 remains enabled. On an internet-facing web server this makes theft of the credentials embedded in user data (and any role credentials) trivial via SSRF. Reviewer B's higher severity is justified because the user data explicitly contains secrets reachable through IMDS.
No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so unless the AMI enforces it the instance root volume is stored unencrypted at rest.

The instance is launched in a subnet with map_public_ip_on_launch enabled and routed directly to an internet gateway, placing the host directly on the internet with no load balancer, NAT, or bastion boundary in front of it.
The EBS volume attached to the portal server does not set encrypted = true or a kms_key_id, leaving the stored data unencrypted at rest.
The snapshot is derived from an unencrypted EBS volume and is therefore itself unencrypted; snapshots can be copied or shared across accounts, broadening exposure of the plaintext data.
The VPC flow log destination bucket has no server-side encryption configuration (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS), so sensitive network telemetry is stored without enforced encryption or key control.

No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, ACL, or bucket policy constrains the flow log bucket, leaving protection of network traffic records entirely dependent on account-level defaults. Medium rather than high is appropriate as no policy in this configuration actually grants public access.
There is no bucket policy denying requests where aws:SecureTransport is false, permitting flow log objects to be written or retrieved over cleartext HTTP connections.

force_destroy = true with no versioning, MFA delete, or object lock allows the audit-relevant flow log archive and all of its objects to be silently and irrecoverably deleted, undermining the integrity of security logging.
map_public_ip_on_launch = true causes every instance launched in this subnet to receive a public IP address, removing the network boundary for all workloads placed there by default.
map_public_ip_on_launch = true causes every instance launched in this subnet to receive a public IP address, removing the network boundary for all workloads placed there by default.

The single route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway and is associated with both subnets, so the VPC contains no private tier; every workload deployed into it is directly internet-reachable. Reviewer B is correct to flag this as an architectural absence of network segmentation.
